reading.rtitle: Your Career in Two Minutes: How to Tell Your Story at a Business Meeting
paras: At an international meeting, the first question is often not about prices. It is personal: "So, how did you get into this field?" Many professionals avoid giving details. They say their job title and stop talking. But your counterpart wants to hear a story, because people trust a story more than a title.

A good career story has four parts. First, how it all started: what you wanted to do when you were young. Second, a turning point: a moment that changed your direction. Third, a milestone or an accomplishment you are proud of, for example the day you moved up to director. Finally, your drive: what makes you keep working hard. Try to finish in two minutes, and practice telling it out loud before the trip.

Claudia Ramos, a Brazilian engineer who oversees four factories, remembers her first meeting in Texas. "I decided to tell the truth," she says. "I told them that I started in a lab, that I never planned to be a manager, and that I agreed to take on a factory in a very demanding year. They stopped looking at their phones. At the end, they told me they enjoyed listening to my story, and we managed to close the deal the next month. Now I love telling that story. It is the most rewarding part of every meeting."

listenings.text: Hi Lucimara, it's Tom Reyes. I really enjoyed meeting you at the reception last night. Small change for tomorrow: I'd like to move our meeting to breakfast at eight, at the cafe in your hotel. My boss, Linda, decided to join us, because she oversees all our purchasing in Latin America. Before we talk about numbers, she wants to hear your story: how you got into the chemical field and how you moved up in your company. Oh, and please remember to bring the samples of your new product. We're hoping to sign something before the end of the year. See you tomorrow!

When I was twenty-two, I wanted to be a chemistry teacher. I enjoyed working in the lab, and I never planned to work in business. The turning point came when I was twenty-eight. My manager asked me to take on a project in Mexico. I was afraid, but I agreed to go. That year was very demanding. I spent months traveling between three factories, and I kept making mistakes in Spanish. But I learned to listen. Five years later, I moved up to plant manager, and today I oversee eleven plants in four countries. My biggest accomplishment? Building a team that doesn't need me in the room. And my drive? I love solving problems. The most rewarding part of my job is watching young engineers grow.

extra_audio.text: First, I say how it all started. Then, I talk about a turning point in my career. Next, I mention a milestone I'm proud of. After that, I explain what I do today. Finally, I say what drives me.
